parts.title: The Future Of World Languages
parts.article:
(A) Of the world’s 6,500 living languages, around half are expected to die out by the end of this century, according to UNESCO. Just 11 are spoken by more than half of the earth’s population, so it is little wonder that those used by only a few are being left behind as we become a more homogenous, global society. In short, 95 percent of the world’s languages are spoken by only five percent of its population—a remarkable level of linguistic diversity stored in tiny pockets of speakers around the world. Mark Turin, a university professor, has launched WOLP (World Oral Language Project) to prevent the language from the brink of extinction.

(B) He is trying to encourage indigenous communities to collaborate with anthropologists around the world to record what he calls “oral literature” through video cameras, voice recorders and other multimedia tools by awarding grants from a £30,000 pot that the project has secured this year. The idea is to collate this literature in a digital archive that can be accessed on demand and will make the nuts and bolts of lost cultures readily available.

(C) For many of these communities, the oral tradition is at the heart of their culture. The stories they tell are creative as well as communicative. Unlike the languages with celebrated written traditions, such as Sanskrit, Hebrew and Ancient Greek, few indigenous communities have recorded their own languages or ever had them recorded until now.

(D) The project suggested itself when Turin was teaching in Nepal. He wanted to study for a PhD in endangered languages and, while discussing it with his professor at Leiden University in the Netherlands, was drawn to a map on his tutor’s wall. The map was full of pins of a variety of colours which represented all the world’s languages that were completely undocumented. At random, Turin chose a “pin” to document. It happened to belong to the Thangmi tribe, an indigenous community in the hills east of Kathmandu, the capital of Nepal. “Many of the choices anthropologists and linguists who work on these traditional field-work projects are quite random,” he admits.

(E) Continuing his work with the Thangmi community in the 1990s, Turin began to record the language he was hearing, realising that not only was this language and its culture entirely undocumented, it was known to few outside the tiny community. He set about trying to record their language and myth of origins. “I wrote 1,000 pages of grammar in English that nobody could use—but I realised that wasn’t enough. It wasn’t enough for me, it wasn’t enough for them. It simply wasn’t going to work as something for the community. So then I produced this trilingual word list in Thangmi, Nepali and English.”

(F) In short, it was the first ever publication of that language. That small dictionary is still sold in local schools for a modest 20 rupees, and used as part of a wider cultural regeneration process to educate children about their heritage and language. The task is no small undertaking: Nepal itself is a country of massive ethnic and linguistic diversity, home to 100 languages from four different language families. What’s more, even fewer ethnic Thangmi speak the Thangmi language. Many of the community members have taken to speaking Nepali, the national language taught in schools and spread through the media, and community elders are dying without passing on their knowledge.

(G) Despite Turin’s enthusiasm for his subject, he is baffled by many linguists’ refusal to engage in the issue he is working on. “Of the 6,500 languages spoken on Earth, many do not have written traditions and many of these spoken forms are endangered,” he says. “There are more linguists in universities around the world than there are spoken languages—but most of them aren’t working on this issue. To me it’s amazing that in this day and age, we still have an entirely incomplete image of the world’s linguistic diversity. People do PhDs on the apostrophe in French, yet we still don’t know how many languages are spoken.”

(H) “When a language becomes endangered, so too does a cultural world view. We want to engage with indigenous people to document their myths and folklore, which can be harder to find funding for if you are based outside Western universities.”

(I) Yet, despite the struggles facing initiatives such as the World Oral Literature Project, there are historical examples that point to the possibility that language restoration is no mere academic pipe dream. The revival of a modern form of Hebrew in the 19th century is often cited as one of the best proofs that languages long dead, belonging to small communities, can be resurrected and embraced by a large number of people. By the 20th century, Hebrew was well on its way to becoming the main language of the Jewish population of both Ottoman and British Palestine. It is now spoken by more than seven million people in Israel.

(J) Yet, despite the difficulties these communities face in saving their languages, Dr Turin believes that the fate of the world’s endangered languages is not sealed, and globalisation is not necessarily the nefarious perpetrator of evil it is often presented to be. “I call it the globalisation paradox: on the one hand globalisation and rapid socio-economic change are the things that are eroding and challenging diversity. But on the other, globalisation is providing us with new and very exciting tools and facilities to get to places to document those things that globalisation is eroding. Also, the communities at the coal-face of change are excited by what globalisation has to offer.”

(K) In the meantime, the race is on to collect and protect as many of the languages as possible, so that the Rai Shaman in eastern Nepal and those in the generations that follow him can continue their traditions and have a sense of identity. And it certainly is a race: Turin knows his project’s limits and believes it inevitable that a large number of those languages will disappear. “We have to be wholly realistic. A project like ours is in no position, and was not designed, to keep languages alive. The only people who can help languages survive are the people in those communities themselves. They need to be reminded that it’s good to speak their own language and I think we can help them do that—becoming modern doesn’t mean you have to lose your language.”

Questions 27–31
Complete the summary using the list of words, A-J, below.
Write the correct letter, A-J, in boxes 27–31 on your answer sheet.
Of the world’s 6,500 living languages, about half of them are expected to be extinct. Most of the world’s languages are spoken by a of people. However, Professor Turin set up a project WOLP to prevent of the languages. The project provides the community with to enable people to record their endangered languages. The oral tradition has great cultural . An important between languages spoken by few people and languages with celebrated written documents existed in many communities.
  • A similarity
  • B significance
  • C funding
  • D minority
  • E education
  • F difference
  • G education
  • H diversity
  • I majority
  • J disappearance
Questions 32–35
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 32–35 on your answer sheet, write.

Q32 Turin argued that anthropologists and linguists usually think carefully before selecting an area to research.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q33 Turin concluded that the Thangmi language had few similarities with other languages.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q34 Turin has written that 1000-page document was inappropriate for Thangmi community;

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q35 Some Nepalese schools lack resources to devote to language teaching.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 36–40
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 36–40 on your answer sheet.

Q36 Why does Turin say people do PhDs on the apostrophe in French?

  • A He believes that researchers have limited role in the research of languages.
  • B He compares the methods of research into languages.
  • C He thinks research should result in a diverse cultural outlook.
  • D He holds that research into French should focus on more general aspects.

Q37 What is discussed in the ninth paragraph?

  • A Forces driving people to believe endangered languages can survive.
  • B The community where people distrust language revival.
  • C The methods of research that have improved language restoration.
  • D Initiatives the World Oral Literature Project is bringing to Israel.

Q38 How is the WOLP’s prospect?

  • A It would not raise enough funds to achieve its aims.
  • B It will help keep languages alive.
  • C It will be embraced by a large number of people.
  • D It has chance to succeed to protect the endangered languages.

Q39 What is Turin’s main point of globalisation?

  • A Globalisation is the main reason for endangered language.
  • B Globalisation has both advantages and disadvantages.
  • C We should have a more critical view of globalisation.
  • D We should foremost protect our identity in face of globalisation.

Q40 What does Turin suggest that community people should do?

  • A Learn other languages.
  • B Only have a sense of identity.
  • C Keep up with the modern society without losing their language.
  • D Join the race to protect as many languages as possible but be realistic.

reference:
Q27

解析 原文明确提到世界上95%的语言只有5%的人在使用，这5%的人口完美对应选项D的“少数人（minority）”。

干扰 你可能会因为看到“95 percent”而下意识想选代表“多数”的选项I（majority），但题目问的是“说这些语言的人口”占多少，必须紧盯“five percent”。

句子 In short, 95 percent of the world’s languages are spoken by only five percent of its population—a remarkable level of linguistic diversity stored in tiny pockets of speakers around the world.

Q28

解析 原文说设立WOLP项目是为了防止语言走向“灭绝（extinction）”，对应选项J的“消失（disappearance）”。

干扰 你可能会被前面的“prevent”带偏去盲目找生词，但其实这道题只是单纯考查你是否知道 extinction 和 disappearance 是最直接的同义替换。

句子 Mark Turin, a university professor, has launched WOLP (World Oral Language Project) to prevent the language from the brink of extinction.

Q29

解析 原文指出项目通过颁发3万英镑的“补助金（grants）”来鼓励大家记录语言，这对应选项C的“资金（funding）”。

干扰 你可能会看到原文的录像机、录音机就想找“设备”类的选项，但项目真正作为奖金发放给当地人的核心支持是钱（grants）。

句子 He is trying to encourage indigenous communities to collaborate with anthropologists around the world to record what he calls “oral literature” through video cameras, voice recorders and other multimedia tools by awarding grants from a £30,000 pot that the project has secured this year.

Q30

解析 原文提到口述传统是当地文化的“核心（at the heart of）”，意味着它具有极大的“重要性（significance）”，对应选项B。

干扰 你可能会因为后面常常跟着文化一词而想猜“多样性（diversity）”，但原文强调的是口述传统在文化里无可替代的核心地位。

句子 For many of these communities, the oral tradition is at the heart of their culture. The stories they tell are creative as well as communicative.

Q31

解析 原文开头的“Unlike（不同于）”直接点明了有书面传统的语言和极少被记录的土著语言之间存在着显著的“差异（difference）”，对应选项F。

干扰 你可能会被句子中间各种复杂的语言名字绕晕，但这句打头的一个“Unlike”就已经亮明了强烈的对比关系，千万别看反了去选“相似性（similarity）”。

句子 Unlike the languages with celebrated written traditions, such as Sanskrit, Hebrew and Ancient Greek, few indigenous communities have recorded their own languages or ever had them recorded until now.

Q32

解析 题目说人类学家选研究区域时通常会“深思熟虑（think carefully）”，而原文说这些选择其实非常“随机（quite random）”，两者意思完全相反。

干扰 你可能会根据常理认为做学术研究肯定得深思熟虑，但在阅读考试中必须严格以原文给出的“random（随机）”这个词为唯一标准，不能自己加戏。

句子 “Many of the choices anthropologists and linguists who work on these traditional field-work projects are quite random,” he admits.

Q33

解析 原文只提到了这门语言完全没有被记录过且鲜为人知，但通篇根本没有提过它和其他语言相比是否有“相似处（similarities）”。

干扰 你可能会因为原文说它“鲜有人知”就自己脑补它很独特、和其他语言都不像，这种无中生有的推断是做 NOT GIVEN 题目时最容易踩的坑。

句子 Continuing his work with the Thangmi community in the 1990s, Turin began to record the language he was hearing, realising that not only was this language and its culture entirely undocumented, it was known to few outside the tiny community. He set about trying to record their language and myth of origins.

Q34

解析 原文里作者承认自己写的1000页语法书“没人能用”，且对当地社区来说“行不通（wasn't going to work）”，这和题目里的“不合适（inappropriate）”完美对应。

干扰 你可能会觉得“inappropriate”太正式，而原文说得像口头大白话，一时没敢确认它们在语境下其实就是同义替换。

句子 “I wrote 1,000 pages of grammar in English that nobody could use—but I realised that wasn’t enough. It wasn’t enough for me, it wasn’t enough for them. It simply wasn’t going to work as something for the community.”

Q35

解析 原文提到了学校卖廉价字典以及教授国家语言，但没有任何一个字眼提到尼泊尔的学校“缺乏资源（lack resources）”来进行教学。

干扰 你可能会看到字典只卖不起眼的“20卢比”就联想到当地学校很穷、没资源，但这属于完全偏离原文事实的过度猜测。

句子 That small dictionary is still sold in local schools for a modest 20 rupees, and used as part of a wider cultural regeneration process to educate children about their heritage and language. ... Many of the community members have taken to speaking Nepali, the national language taught in schools and spread through the media, and community elders are dying without passing on their knowledge.

Q36

解析 原文用人们去专门研究“法语撇号”这种细枝末节做例子，是为了批评许多学者没有把精力放在拯救濒危语言的大问题上，说明作者认为目前研究人员发挥的作用非常“有限（limited role）”。

干扰 你可能会去死抠字眼想选D（觉得对法语的研究应该更全面），但作者举这个例子纯粹是为了讽刺学术界避重就轻的现象，根本不是在真诚探讨法语该怎么研究。

句子 “There are more linguists in universities around the world than there are spoken languages—but most of them aren’t working on this issue. To me it’s amazing that in this day and age, we still have an entirely incomplete image of the world’s linguistic diversity. People do PhDs on the apostrophe in French, yet we still don’t know how many languages are spoken.”

Q37

解析 本段一开头就指出，历史上的成功案例（如希伯来语的复兴）证明了恢复濒危语言并非做梦，这些案例就是让人相信语言能存活的“推动力（Forces driving people to believe...）”。

干扰 你可能会一看到希伯来语就想去找具体的复兴“方法（methods）”，但这整个段落的核心是利用成功案例来给人们打气、传递希望，而不是在教具体的操作手段。

句子 Yet, despite the struggles facing initiatives such as the World Oral Literature Project, there are historical examples that point to the possibility that language restoration is no mere academic pipe dream. The revival of a modern form of Hebrew in the 19th century is often cited as one of the best proofs that languages long dead, belonging to small communities, can be resurrected and embraced by a large number of people.

Q38

解析 原文提到Turin博士认为濒危语言的命运“并未注定（not sealed）”，这种态度表明他认为项目在保护语言方面依然有成功的“机会（chance to succeed）”。

干扰 你可能会看到最后一段说项目本身无法让语言直接活下去就灰心选了A（资金不足），但原文核心意思是真正让语言活下去得靠当地人，而项目“保护记录”的初衷依然大有希望。

句子 Yet, despite the difficulties these communities face in saving their languages, Dr Turin believes that the fate of the world’s endangered languages is not sealed, and globalisation is not necessarily the nefarious perpetrator of evil it is often presented to be.

Q39

解析 原文明确把全球化称为“悖论”，指出它一方面在侵蚀多样性，另一方面又提供了记录语言的新工具，完美印证了“既有好处也有坏处（both advantages and disadvantages）”。

干扰 你可能会只看前半句觉得全球化是个彻头彻尾的坏东西（误选A），但在雅思长难句里，转折词“But on the other”后面的优点才是决定全局走向的关键信息。

句子 “I call it the globalisation paradox: on the one hand globalisation and rapid socio-economic change are the things that are eroding and challenging diversity. But on the other, globalisation is providing us with new and very exciting tools and facilities to get to places to document those things that globalisation is eroding.”

Q40

解析 原文最后一句话直击要害：“走向现代化并不意味着你必须失去你的语言”，这和选项C的“跟上现代社会步伐同时不丢失语言”完全对应。

干扰 你可能会受选项D中“protect...languages”的迷惑，但原文明确说了“去赛跑保护语言”是项目团队的事，对“当地社区群众”的具体建议则是在现代化中留住自己的母语。

句子 The only people who can help languages survive are the people in those communities themselves. They need to be reminded that it’s good to speak their own language and I think we can help them do that—becoming modern doesn’t mean you have to lose your language.”
